source_text: Ἐκεῖ νοι γὰρ, εἰ καί τι τῶν ἀναγκαίων ἐπὶ τῆς νηὸς ἄγον τες τύχοιεν, κλύδων δὲ ἐπαναστῇ ζέων ἐκ τοῦ πελά γους αὐτοῖς, καὶ καλύπτειν ἀπειλήσῃ πεπιεσμέ νην τῷ φόρτῳ τὴν ναῦν, ὅπως ἔχουσι τάχους, τὸ πολὺ τοῦ βάρους ἀποσκευάζουσι, καὶ τὴν ἐμπορίαν ἀφειδῶς ἀντλοῦσιν εἰς θάλασσαν, ὥστε ὑψηλοτέραν ποιῆσαι τὴν ναῦν τοῦ κύματος, καὶ μόναις ταῖς ψυχαῖς, εἴπερ οἷόν τε, καὶ τοῖς σώμασιν ἐκ τοῦ κινδύνου δοῦναι φυγήν. Πολλῷ δὲ ἐκείνων δήπου μᾶλλον ταῦτα ἡμᾶς βουλεύεσθαί τε προσήκει καὶ πράττειν. Ἐκεῖνοι μὲν γὰρ ὅπερ ἂν ἀποῤῥίψωσιν, εὐθέως ἀπώλεσαν, καὶ περιίσταται λοιπὸν βία πενίας αὐτοῖς· ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐφ' ὅσον ἂν τὸν πονηρὸν ἐξαντλή σωμεν φόρτον, πλείονα καὶ βελτίονα ταῖς ψυχαῖς πλοῦτον ἐπισωρεύσομεν. Πορνεία μὲν γὰρ, καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα, ῥιφέντα διόλλυται, καὶ πρὸς τὸ μηδὲ εἶναι χωρεῖ, λυθέντα τοῖς δάκρυσιν· ἁγιότης δὲ καὶ δι καιοσύνη λοιπὸν εἰς τὸν ἐκείνων μεθίσταται χῶρον, πράγματα κοῦφα, καὶ οὐκ εἰδότα κύμασι καλυφθῆναί τισι. Τὰ χρήματά γε μὴν, ἐκβληθέντα καλῶς, οὔτε ἀπόλλυται τοῖς ἐκβαλοῦσι καὶ ῥίψασιν· ἀλλ', ὥσπερ εἰς ὁλκάδας ἄλλας ἀσφαλεστέρας τινὰς, τὰς τῶν πενήτων μετατεθέντα γαστέρας, διασώζεται καὶ φθάνει πρὸς λιμένας ἐλθόντα, καὶ φυλάττεται τοῖς ἐκβάλλουσι, κόσμος, οὐ κίνδυνος. Βουλευσώμεθα τοίνυν, ἀγαπητοὶ, περὶ ἑαυ τούς τι φιλάνθρωπον, καὶ τὸ τῆς εὐπορίας ἄχθος, εἴπερ ὅλως ἐθέλοιμεν ποιήσασθαι κέρδος ἡμέτερον, πολλοῖς διανείμωμεν, οἳ βαστάσουσί τε αὐτὸ περιχα ρῶς, καὶ τοῖς τοῦ Δεσπότου κόλποις, ἀσύλοις ταμείοις, ἐναποκλείσουσιν, Ὅπου σὴς οὐκ ἀφανίζει, οὐδὲ λῃσταὶ διορύττουσιν, οὐδὲ κλέπτουσι. Δῶ μεν ἐξουσίαν ὑπερχυθῆναι βουλομένῳ πρὸς τοὺς δεομένους τῷ πλούτῳ. Μὴ παραδράμωμεν τοὺς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς ἡμῶν ἔτι καὶ νῦν κειμένους Λαζάρους, μηδὲ τῶν ψιχίων τῆς ἡμετέρας τραπέζης ἀρκούντων αὐτοῖς εἰς κόρον βασκήνωμεν· μηδὲ, τὸν ἀνήμερον ἐκεῖνον ζηλώσαντες πλούσιον, πρὸς τὴν αὐτὴν ἐκείνῳ τῆς γεέννης φλόγα μετέλθωμεν. Ἐπεὶ πολ λὰ μὲν τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ δεηθησόμεθα τότε, πολλὰ δὲ ἑκάστου τῶν βεβιωκότων καλῶς· οὐδὲν δὲ ἔσται κέρδος ἡμῖν τῆς βοῆς· Ἀδελφὸς γὰρ οὐ λυτροῦ ται, λυτρώσεται ἄνθρωπος; Ἐρεῖ δὲ ἕκαστος ἐκείνων ἡμῖν κεκραγώς· Μὴ ζήτει φιλανθρωπίαν, ἢν αὐτὸς ἐφ' ἑτέρων ἠγνόησας· μηδὲ βούλου λαβεῖν οὕτω μεγάλα σὺ τῶν ἐλαττόνων φεισάμενος. Ἀπόλαυε τούτων ὧν ἐν τῷ βίῳ συνέλεξας. Δάκρυε νῦν, ἐπειδὴ τότε δακρύοντα τὸν ἀδελφὸν ὁρῶν οὐκ ἠλέη σας. Ταῦτα ἐροῦσι, καὶ δικαίως, ἡμῖν. Δέδοικα δὲ ἐγὼ, μὴ καὶ πικροτέροις ἡμᾶς τούτων βάλωσι ῥή μασιν, ἐπειδὴ καὶ νικῶμεν ἐκεῖνον, ὡς ἴστε, τῇ πονηρίᾳ τὸν πλούσιον. Οὐδὲ γὰρ φειδόμενοι καθ άπαξ πλούτου, τοὺς ἐῤῥιμμένους χαμαὶ παρατρέχο μεν ἀδελφοὺς, οὐδὲ τοῖς παισὶν ἢ τοῖς ἄλλοις οἰκείοις τὴν εὐπορίαν φυλάττοντες, ἀποκλείομεν τοῖς δεομέ νοις τὰς ἀκοάς· ἀλλὰ τὴν δαπάνην μετατιθέντες ἐπὶ τοῖς χείροσι, καὶ τὸ φιλότιμον ἀκόνην πονηρίας ποιού μενοι τοῖς ταύτην ἐπιτηδεύουσι. Πόσαι γὰρ ἢ πόσοι τῶν ἐνίων περιεστήκασι τράπεζαν! οἱ μὲν αἰσχροῖς ῥήμασι τὸν ἑστιάτορα θέλγοντες, οἱ δὲ ἀτόποις βλέμμασί τε καὶ σχήμασι τὸ τῆς ἀκρασίας ἐκκαίοντες πῦρ· οἱ δὲ τοῖς εἰς ἀλλήλους σκώμμασι γέλωτα τῷ κεκληκότι κατασκευάζειν ἐθέλοντες· ἄλλοι δὲ ἐψευσμένοις ἐπαίνοις ἀπατῶντες αὐτόν.
thought_title: Jettisoning cargo for the soul's safe voyage
orientation: Basil is urging his congregation to imitate sailors who throw cargo overboard in a storm, applying this to giving away wealth before death.
pass_a_gloss: For those men, even if they happen to be carrying some of the necessary things on the ship, and a boiling wave rises up against them from the open sea, and threatens to cover the ship pressed down by the cargo, with as much speed as they have, they throw off the greater part of the weight, and they pour out the merchandise unsparingly into the sea, so as to make the ship higher than the wave, and to give escape from the danger to their souls alone, if possible, and to their bodies. And it is fitting for us, surely, to plan and to do these things much more than those men. For whatever those men throw away, they immediately lose, and the force of poverty remains for them thereafter; but we, for as much as we pour out the wicked cargo, will heap up more and better wealth for our souls. For fornication, and as many things as are of that kind, when thrown away is destroyed, and goes toward not even existing, being dissolved by tears; but holiness and righteousness thereafter pass over into the place of those things, light matters, and not knowing how to be covered by any waves. The money, however, when thrown out well, is not lost to those who throw it out and cast it away; but, just as into other safer ships, into the bellies of the poor, being transferred, it is preserved and arrives first at harbors, and is kept for those who throw it out, an ornament, not a danger. Let us plan, then, beloved, something loving toward ourselves, and let us distribute the burden of abundance, if we really wish to make it our own gain, to many, who will carry it very gladly, and will shut it up in the bosoms of the Master, in inviolable treasuries, where moth does not destroy, nor thieves break in, nor steal. Let us give permission to the wealth that wishes to overflow toward those in need. Let us not run past the Lazaruses lying before our eyes still even now, nor let us begrudge the crumbs of our table being sufficient for them to their fill; nor, having emulated that savage rich man, let us go over to the same flame of hell as that man. Since then we will beg Abraham for many things, and each of those who lived well for many things; and there will be no gain for us from the cry; for a brother does not redeem, shall a man redeem? And each of those men will say to us, crying out: Do not seek the love of humanity that you yourself ignored in the case of others; nor wish to receive such great things, you who spared the lesser things. Enjoy these things which you gathered in life. Weep now, since then, seeing your brother weeping, you did not have mercy. These things they will say to us, and justly. And I fear that they may cast at us words even more bitter than these, since we surpass that rich man in wickedness, as you know. For we do not, sparing wealth altogether, run past our brothers thrown on the ground, nor, keeping our abundance for our children or our other relatives, do we shut our ears to those in need; but, transferring our expenditure to worse things, and making our love of honor a whetstone of wickedness for those who practice it. For how many women or how many men of some people stand around the table! Some charming the host with shameful words, others kindling the fire of incontinence with improper glances and gestures; others wishing to produce laughter for the one who invited them with mockeries against one another; and others deceiving him with false praises.

choices.why: Dative singular masculine participle modifying τῷ πλούτῳ (the wealth), personifying wealth as wishing to overflow; not 'as we desire'.
Partitive genitive plural of ἔνιοι ('some, certain people'); Basil asks how many women or men of certain people stand around the table, implying the hosts among his hearers.
Neuter plural genitive of ἐλάττων, referring to small acts of mercy or small possessions, not people.

Adverb meaning 'altogether, absolutely'; with the negative it means 'not at all', but the construction 'οὐδὲ γὰρ...καθάπαξ' means 'for not even...altogether', i.e., they do not even do the minimal thing of sparing wealth and passing by.
Metaphor: their love of honor sharpens wickedness in those who practice it, like a whetstone sharpens a blade.

pass_b_english: Those sailors, you see, if they happen to be carrying even some necessary cargo on board and a boiling swell rises against them from the open sea and threatens to sink the ship, weighed down as it is by its load, throw off most of the weight as fast as they can. They pour their merchandise into the sea without mercy, so as to raise the ship above the waves and, if possible, bring only their souls and bodies safely out of danger. How much more, then, should we plan and do these very things! For whatever those men throw overboard they lose at once, and from then on the force of poverty closes in on them. But the more of our wicked cargo we pour out, the more and better wealth we will heap up for our souls. Fornication and all such things, once thrown off, are destroyed and pass into nothingness, dissolved by tears. But holiness and righteousness pass over into the place of those very things—light possessions that no waves can cover. Money, however, when thrown out well, is not lost to those who throw it out and cast it away. Rather, as if transferred into other, safer ships—the stomachs of the poor—it is preserved and arrives first at the harbor, and it is kept for those who throw it out as an ornament, not a danger. Let us then, beloved, plan something philanthropic for ourselves, and if we truly want to make the burden of our abundance our own gain, let us distribute it among many who will carry it joyfully and lock it away in the bosom of the Master, in treasuries that cannot be plundered—where moth does not destroy, and thieves do not break in and steal (Matthew 6:20). Let us give our wealth permission to overflow toward those in need. Let us not run past the Lazaruses who even now lie before our eyes, nor begrudge them the crumbs from our table that would satisfy them. Let us not imitate that savage rich man and go over with him into the same flame of hell. For then we will beg Abraham at length, and beg at length each of those who lived well, but our shouting will gain us nothing. “A brother cannot redeem; can a man redeem?” (Psalm 48:8 (49:7)). Each of those people will cry out to us and say: “Do not seek the mercy you yourself ignored when others needed it. Do not expect to receive such great things, you who spared the lesser ones. Enjoy what you gathered in life. Weep now, since you did not pity your brother when you saw him weeping then.” These things they will say to us, and justly. But I am afraid they may hurl even harsher words at us, because, as you know, we surpass that rich man in wickedness. For not sparing our wealth at all, we run past our brothers thrown on the ground, and while keeping our abundance for our children or other relatives, we shut our ears to those in need. Instead, we transfer our spending to worse things and make our love of honor a whetstone of wickedness for those who practice it. For how many women or how many men of certain people stand around the table! Some charm the host with shameful words, others kindle the fire of self-indulgence with indecent glances and gestures, others want to produce laughter for the one who invited them by mocking one another, and still others deceive him with false praises.

problems.why: βουλομένῳ is dative masculine, agreeing with πλούτῳ (wealth), not a neuter 'as it wishes'; the sense is 'to wealth that wishes/desires to overflow', personifying wealth's natural tendency.
problems.fix: to wealth that longs to overflow toward those in need

problems.source_quote: Βουλευσώμεθα τοίνυν, ἀγαπητοί, περὶ ἑαυτούς τι φιλάνθρωπον
problems.why: φιλάνθρωπον means 'loving toward humanity/philanthropic,' not 'toward ourselves.' Basil urges planning something humane for others.
problems.fix: Let us then, beloved, plan something philanthropic for ourselves

problems.quote: Do not expect to receive such great things, you who spared the lesser things.
problems.source_quote: μηδὲ βούλου λαβεῖν οὕτω μεγάλα σὺ τῶν ἐλαττόνων φεισάμενος.
problems.why: τῶν ἐλαττόνων means 'the lesser ones' (the poor), not 'the lesser things.' The rebuke is: you who spared the poor should not expect great rewards.
problems.fix: Do not expect to receive such great things, you who spared the lesser ones.
problems.ruling: τῶν ἐλαττόνων = 'the lesser/poorer ones' (people), not 'lesser things.'

problems.quote: Weep now, since when you saw your brother weeping then, you had no pity.
problems.source_quote: Δάκρυε νῦν, ἐπειδὴ τότε δακρύοντα τὸν ἀδελφὸν ὁρῶν οὐκ ἠλέη σας.
problems.why: Source says 'when you saw your brother weeping then' — the 'then' (τότε) referring to the past time of need is dropped, losing the temporal contrast with 'now.'
problems.fix: Weep now, since you did not pity your brother when you saw him weeping then.
problems.ruling: τότε ('then') dropped, losing temporal contrast with νῦν ('now').

problems.quote: For we do not even spare our wealth altogether and run past our brothers thrown on the ground
problems.source_quote: Οὐδὲ γὰρ φειδόμενοι καθάπαξ πλούτου, τοὺς ἐῤῥιμμένους χαμαὶ παρατρέχομεν ἀδελφούς
problems.why: Source says 'we DO spare wealth and run past brothers.' The οὐδέ governs only the second clause: 'we do not run past brothers while sparing wealth.'
problems.fix: For while sparing our wealth altogether, we run past our brothers thrown on the ground
problems.ruling: οὐδέ negates παρατρέχομεν, not φειδόμενοι: 'not running past brothers while sparing wealth.'

problems.quote: nor do we keep our abundance for our children or other relatives and shut our ears to those in need

problems.why: Source says 'we DO keep abundance for children/relatives and shut ears to those in need.' The οὐδέ governs only the second verb: 'we do not shut ears while keeping abundance.'
problems.fix: nor, while keeping our abundance for our children or other relatives, do we shut our ears to those in need
problems.ruling: οὐδέ negates ἀποκλείομεν, not φυλάττοντες: 'not shutting ears while keeping abundance.'

fixed: βουλομένῳ is dative masculine agreeing with πλούτῳ, so 'to wealth that longs to overflow' is correct.
φιλάνθρωπον means philanthropic/humane, not 'toward ourselves'; edited.
τῶν ἐλαττόνων means 'the lesser ones' (the poor), not 'the lesser things'; edited.
τότε was dropped; restored the temporal contrast.

problems.quote: to wealth that longs to overflow toward those in need
problems.source_quote: Δῶμεν ἐξουσίαν ὑπερχυθῆναι βουλομένῳ πρὸς τοὺς δεομένους τῷ πλούτῳ
problems.why: The Greek says 'let us give permission to the wealth that longs to overflow toward those in need,' not 'to wealth that longs to overflow.' The English adds an extra 'to wealth that longs' phrase, making it seem like two actions rather than one.
problems.fix: Let us give our wealth permission to overflow toward those in need.

problems.why: καθάπαξ means 'at all, in any way' (with οὐδὲ = 'not at all'), not 'altogether.' The sense is 'not sparing wealth at all'—they're not even trying to be stingy; they just ignore the poor. The English 'altogether' suggests total sparing/total stinginess, which is opposite.
problems.fix: not sparing our wealth at all

problems.quote: do we shut our ears to those in need
problems.why: The Greek says 'we shut our ears to those in need,' but the context with οὐδὲ...ἀποκλείομεν means 'nor do we shut our ears.' However, the preceding clause has οὐδὲ...παρατρέχομεν, and the whole section is a list of things they DON'T do (introduced by οὐδὲ). Wait—let me re-read: the structure is 'οὐδὲ...παρατρέχομεν...οὐδὲ...ἀποκλείομεν'—both negated. But then ἀλλὰ introduces the actual bad behavior. So 'we do not run past...nor do we shut our ears'—but this is sarcastic? No, looking again: the ἀλλὰ clause reveals the truth: 'but we transfer our spending to worse things.' So the οὐδὲ clauses are stating what they fail to do (negatively framed). Actually, re-reading: 'For while not sparing wealth at all, we run past our brothers...nor, while keeping abundance for children, do we shut our ears to those in need; but we transfer spending to worse things.' This is confusing—the Greek seems to say they DO run past brothers and DO shut ears, but the grammar has οὐδὲ. Wait—οὐδὲ γὰρ φειδόμενοι...οὐδὲ τοῖς παισὶν...τὴν εὐπορίαν φυλάττοντες, ἀποκλείομεν. The οὐδὲ before τοῖς παισὶν coordinates with the first οὐδὲ, but there's no negative verb. Actually, I think the οὐδὲ is 'and not/nor' continuing a negative thought, but the main verb παρατρέχομεν is positive. This is a known crux. But the English 'do we shut our ears' with 'nor' makes it a question/negative, which doesn't match if the Greek means 'we shut our ears.' Let me re-check: 'οὐδὲ...παρατρέχομεν'—οὐδὲ + indicative can mean 'and not' or 'nor.' But παρατρέχομεν is positive form. So 'nor do we run past' = 'we do not run past.' Then 'οὐδὲ...ἀποκλείομεν' = 'nor do we shut.' But this contradicts the ἀλλὰ clause. Unless it's irony? Actually, I think the English is wrong: it should be 'we run past' and 'we shut our ears'—the οὐδὲ is misplaced or the text is corrupt, but the sense from the ἀλλὰ clause is that they DO these bad things. The English makes them sound like they don't shut their ears, which contradicts the argument.
problems.fix: nor, while keeping our abundance for our children or other relatives, do we open our ears to those in need

edits.old: Let us give our wealth permission to overflow toward those in need, to wealth that longs to overflow toward those in need.
edits.new: Let us give our wealth permission to overflow toward those in need.

edits.old: For while sparing our wealth altogether, we run past our brothers thrown on the ground, nor, while keeping our abundance for our children or other relatives, do we shut our ears to those in need.
edits.new: For not sparing our wealth at all, we run past our brothers thrown on the ground, nor, while keeping our abundance for our children or other relatives, do we shut our ears to those in need.

fixed: The addition problem is real: the English duplicates the phrase 'to wealth that longs to overflow toward those in need,' which is not in the source. The source has only one clause: 'Δῶμεν ἐξουσίαν ὑπερχυθῆναι βουλομένῳ πρὸς τοὺς δεομένους τῷ πλούτῳ' = 'Let us give permission to the wealth that wishes to overflow toward those in need.' Removed the duplicate.

The mistranslation of καθάπαξ is real: καθάπαξ means 'at all, in any way,' not 'altogether.' The source phrase 'οὐδὲ γὰρ φειδόμενοι καθάπαξ πλούτου' means 'for not sparing wealth at all,' not 'while sparing our wealth altogether.' Changed 'while sparing our wealth altogether' to 'not sparing our wealth at all.'

The reported problem about 'do we shut our ears' is not a mistranslation. The source has 'οὐδὲ...ἀποκλείομεν τοῖς δεομένοις τὰς ἀκοάς' = 'nor do we shut our ears to those in need.' The English correctly renders this as 'nor...do we shut our ears.' The suggested fix 'do we open our ears' would reverse the meaning and contradict the source. No edit made.

problems.quote: nor, while keeping our abundance for our children or other relatives, do we shut our ears to those in need.
problems.why: Source says we DO shut our ears to those in need; English negates it, flipping the meaning.
problems.fix: and while keeping our abundance for our children or other relatives, we shut our ears to those in need.
problems.ruling: Source ἀποκλείομεν = 'we shut out'; English 'do we shut' with 'nor' creates double negative, flipping meaning to 'we do NOT shut our ears'.

problems.source_quote: Ὅπου σὴς οὐκ ἀφανίζει, οὐδὲ λῃσταὶ διορύττουσιν, οὐδὲ κλέπτουσιν
problems.why: The Greek quotes Matthew 6:19-20, but the citation should be Matthew 6:19 (or 6:19-20), not 6:20 alone. The verse about moth and thieves is Matthew 6:19 in standard numbering; 6:20 begins "but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven."
problems.ruling: Moth and thieves corrupting treasure = Matt 6:19, not 6:20. Citation is wrong; 6:20 is about heavenly treasures.

edits.old: nor, while keeping our abundance for our children or other relatives, do we shut our ears to those in need.
edits.new: and while keeping our abundance for our children or other relatives, we shut our ears to those in need.

fixed: Negation fixed: source says 'ἀποκλείομεν τοῖς δεομένοις τὰς ἀκοάς' (we shut our ears to those in need), so the English must be affirmative.
Scripture citation fixed: the quoted words about moth and thieves are Matthew 6:19 in standard numbering, not 6:20.

fixed.note: The words 'where moth does not destroy and thieves do not break in' are the negative form, which is Matthew 6:20; verse 19 is the positive warning.

The English rendering of the verse is fine, but the reference gives only the Hebrew-based number and breaks the site's 'LXX number (Hebrew number)' format; the checker's claim about λυτροῦται is wrong.

dismissed.quote: we surpass that rich man in wickedness
dismissed.why: νικῶμεν means 'we conquer/defeat,' not 'surpass.' The point is they beat the rich man at his own game of wickedness—a shocking paradox, not mere comparison.
dismissed.note: Here νικῶμεν with τῇ πονηρίᾳ means 'we outdo him in wickedness', so 'surpass' is accurate and reads better than 'defeat'.
